mainEntity.name: What's the difference between scientific and engineering notation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard scientific notation always has exactly one digit before the decimal point. Engineering notation instead forces the exponent to a multiple of 3, so the mantissa can have 1, 2 or 3 digits before the point — this matches SI prefixes like kilo (10³) and mega (10⁶) directly.

mainEntity.name: Why do calculators and programs write "e" instead of "× 10"?

acceptedAnswer.text: "e" notation (like 4.582e-5) is a plain-text way to write scientific notation without special symbols, used across programming languages, spreadsheets and calculator displays — mathematically it means exactly the same as 4.582 × 10⁻⁵.

mainEntity.name: How does multiplying in scientific notation work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the mantissas and add the exponents: (a×10ᵐ)×(b×10ⁿ) = (a×b)×10ᵐ⁺ⁿ. If the mantissa product is 10 or more (or less than 1), renormalize by shifting the decimal point and adjusting the exponent.

mainEntity.name: Why use scientific notation at all?

acceptedAnswer.text: It makes very large or very small numbers compact and easy to compare — and it separates the number's precision (the mantissa's significant figures) from its scale (the exponent), which is why it's the standard in science and engineering.

mainEntity.name: How is rounding handled when converting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using exact half-to-even (banker's) rounding on the digit string itself — not on a floating-point approximation — so results match the textbook rule precisely, including for ties.
